newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Finland worried by slow pace of EU talks.
newsitem.headline: France, Finland worried by slow pace of EU talks.

text.p: France and Finland expressed concern on Thursday about the European Union's sluggish pace in overhauling its institutions but disagreed about a French plan to axe top jobs at the European Commission.

"France is worried about the timetable" for the 15-member bloc's review of its institutions, due to be completed by mid-1997, Finnish Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said after talks with President Jacques Chirac and Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
"It's very slow," Lipponen told a news conference.
The so-called inter-governmental conference aims to overhaul the workings of the EU to prepare for enlargement towards eastern Europe and the Mediterranean.

A spokesman for Chirac quoted him as saying he hoped an EU summit this weekend in Dublin would allow the timetable to be respected and that a list of issues and solutions would be drawn up "to give foreign ministers a mission".

Juppe expressed optimism about the timetable. He said that cooperation between France and Germany, the main axis of the EU, aimed not to force the timetable but to follow a programme that has already been fixed.

Lipponen said he disagreed with Chirac and Juppe -- who cancelled a lunch with the Finnish premier last year after Helsinki criticised French nuclear tests -- over plans by Paris for a cut in the size of the European Commission, the EU's executive.
"It's France's proposal that we limit the number of Commissioners to eight, maybe 10 at most," Lipponen said. All EU states now have at least one member on the 20-strong executive.
"It's very, very difficult, impossible, to imagine that we would not have a member," Lipponen said.
"The Commission represents a certain objectivity in the union, defending common standards."
He said he was optimistic that there would be a compromise, however.

Lipponen also said the three Baltic States should not get left behind in talks on enlarging the European Union and NATO, and EU nations should avoid picking "political favourites" among countries wanting to join.
He said Chirac "expressed his willingness to increase bilateral contacts with Finland and I expressed our wish that France could engage more in cooperation around the Baltic Sea".
